dev_facts.fact: Our clinical evidence is an external test set of 2000 dermatoscopic images showing 90% melanoma sensitivity and 78% specificity; we have not run a prospective study in real GP practice yet, and I know an external test set isn't the same thing as a prospective trial.

We haven't formally defined contraindications or exclusion criteria yet. The app will classify any lesion photo a GP feeds it — we don't currently screen out or refuse the harder lesion types where I'd expect our model to be weaker, and we don't surface a 'low confidence, do not rely on this' state.

Our EfficientNet-B4 was fine-tuned and tested on dermatoscopic ISIC images, but in the product the GP takes an ordinary smartphone photo at the practice, so the real-world capture conditions (lighting, focus, no dermatoscope) differ from our validation data and we haven't quantified the accuracy drop from that yet.

Consent is a paper form the patient signs at the practice and the app just stores a flag; it's not a granular flow and we rely on the GP to explain it rather than presenting plain-language consent in the app itself.

Photos are stored pseudonymized for 5 years for retraining, retention is a separate opt-in consent the patient can decline or later withdraw, but I'll admit we haven't fully built out or documented the GDPR erasure-on-request workflow, including pulling images already in a retraining set.

The GP enters their clinical impression and then sees our label, but we don't force the impression to be locked in before the prediction is shown, so I can't rule out that some GPs anchor on our 'urgent' or 'benign' output.

Right now the GP just sees one of three labels — benign, suspicious, or urgent. We have the Platt-calibrated class probabilities internally but don't surface them or a saliency map / Grad-CAM, so there's no visible explanation of why the model picked that class.

We position it as a triage aid for the GP, not a diagnosis, but the only place that's stated is our marketing copy and labeling — the app UI doesn't prominently spell out its limitations or that the GP remains responsible for the final clinical decision.

Our plan is to log every prediction plus the GP's final decision and review performance quarterly; that gives us traceability, though I accept quarterly is slow and we don't yet have live drift or anomaly monitoring.

We fine-tuned on ISIC 2020, which is skewed toward Fitzpatrick I-III light skin. I'll be honest that we expect weaker performance on darker skin tones and we haven't measured or corrected for that bias yet — Fitzpatrick type is only an optional field for us.

We localized the interface to EN, DE, FR, IT for our EU and CH GP users, but since it's clinician-facing and image-based we haven't done cross-cultural validation of the classifier itself across populations.

Our validation reporting is a single aggregate sensitivity/specificity number; we have not yet broken performance down by skin tone, age, sex, or body location, so that representativeness analysis is missing from our current evidence pack.

We treat it as Software as a Medical Device — Class IIa under MDR 2017/745 Rule 11 because it provides diagnostic triage information to inform a clinical decision; I've consulted with regulatory on this classification.
CE marking is in progress, our notified body is designated, and the conformity assessment is underway; we have not completed it, so we're not yet CE-marked for market.

We've focused mainly on the MDR track and haven't yet built out our EU AI Act compliance, even though I'm aware that an AI-aided diagnostic device like ours is treated as a high-risk AI system under Annex III with its own obligations on top of MDR.

Our post-market surveillance plan is to log every prediction alongside the GP's final decision and run a quarterly performance review; we haven't yet set up a formal vigilance / adverse-event reporting channel or real-time monitoring.
